main.t: The cheekbone, which forms much of the outer wall of the orbit (zygomatic bone).

simpler.t: The zygomatic bone is your cheekbone.

deeper.t: Its temporal process forms the front of the zygomatic arch.

facts.t: It forms the cheek, at the outer and lower rim of the orbit.
It forms much of the outer (lateral) wall and outer floor of the orbit.
Behind, its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone.

simpler.t: It is the bone you feel at the top of your cheek, below and beside your eye.

deeper.t: The pterion lies a thumb’s width behind its upward part, about two finger widths above the arch.

items.name: Orbital part
items.t: Forms much of the lateral wall and the lateral floor of the orbit.

items.name: Orbital margin
items.t: The outer and lower rim of the front opening of the orbit.

items.name: Temporal process
items.t: A short projection backwards, forming the front of the zygomatic arch.

items.name: Upward part
items.t: Rises at the outer edge of the orbit; a landmark for finding the pterion.

simpler.t: It has a part that walls in the eye socket and a part that reaches back into the arch.

deeper.t: The arch works like a drawbridge: two processes, one from each bone, meet in the middle.

facts.t: The lateral wall of each orbit angles 45 degrees away from the midline, widening side (peripheral) vision.
The thickened margins of the orbit help protect the eye.
The arch it helps form is a bridge of bone from which a major chewing muscle arises.

simpler.t: It shapes your cheek, guards the side of your eye and anchors a chewing muscle.

items.name: Temporal bone
items.t: Its zygomatic process joins the temporal process to complete the arch.

items.name: Orbit
items.t: Forms its lateral wall and lateral floor; the maxilla forms the inner floor.

items.name: Chewing muscle
items.t: A major muscle that pulls the mandible up in biting and chewing arises from the arch.

items.name: Temporal and infratemporal fossae
items.t: The spaces above and below the arch, filled by chewing muscles.

simpler.t: It joins the temporal bone in the arch and forms the outer wall of the eye socket.

facts.t: Like the other flat bones of the face, it forms directly from membrane (intramembranous ossification).
facts.check: OpenStax 6.4 says the flat bones of the face form from membrane, but 7.5 says the facial bones form from cartilage; which applies to the zygomatic bone needs an approved source.

facts.t: The flat bones of the face are the last to ossify from membrane. They reach adult size at the end of the adolescent growth spurt.

items.injury: A blow to the side of the head, just behind the upward part of the zygomatic bone.
items.damaged: The pterion, with a major artery to the brain’s coverings just inside it.
items.cannotDo: Be left without close watching: a haematoma can build up over hours.
items.why: The pterion is the weakest part of the skull, and bleeding there presses on the brain.

items.injury: A punch or blow to the cheek.
items.damaged: The zygomatic bone or arch breaks and may be pushed inwards.
items.cannotDo: Open the mouth fully, if the broken arch presses on the jaw beneath.
items.why: Part of the mandible and chewing muscles lie just deep to the arch.
items.check: The fracture and its effect on opening the mouth are not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

items.q: Explain how the zygomatic arch is built.
model: It spans from the cheek to just above the ear canal.
At the front is the short temporal process of the zygomatic bone.
Behind is the longer zygomatic process of the temporal bone.
The two join like the ends of a drawbridge.

items.q: Compare the parts the zygomatic bone and the maxilla play in the orbit.
model: The zygomatic bone forms the lateral wall and lateral floor.
The maxilla forms most of the medial floor.
The zygomatic bone also forms the outer, lower rim.
The lateral wall angles outwards, widening side vision.

items.q: Predict how to find the pterion on a living head, using the zygomatic bone.
model: Find the upward part of the zygomatic bone, at the outer edge of the eye.
Move a thumb’s width behind it.
Then about two finger widths above the zygomatic arch.
This is the pterion, the weakest part of the skull.

check.stem: Which bone forms the front of the zygomatic arch?
check.why: The temporal process of the zygomatic bone forms the front of the arch.

check.stem: Which part of the orbit does the zygomatic bone mainly form?
check.why: It forms the lateral wall and lateral floor.

check.stem: What arises from the zygomatic arch?
options: A muscle that pulls the jaw up in chewing
check.why: One of the major muscles that raises the mandible arises from the arch.
